observations.content:
Summary: The speed of light in a vacuum is exactly 299,792,458 m/s, as defined by the International System of Units (SI). This fixed value is used to define the metre as the distance light travels in vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. Since 1983, the metre has been redefined so that the speed of light is precisely this number, and the second is defined by the number of caesium-133 atom transitions.

[1] Speed of light - Wikipedia
    https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_of_light
    The constant c is defined in the International System of Units (SI) as exactly 299792458 m/s. This fixed value is used to define the metre as exactly the distance that light travels in vacuum in 1⁄299792458 of a second. The second is, in turn, defined to be the length of time occupied by 9192631770 cycles of the radiation emitted by a caesium-133 atom in a transition between two specified energy states. By using the fixed value of c and an accurate measurement of the second, the value for the [...] As a result of this definition, the value of the speed of light in vacuum is exactly 299792458 m/s and has become a defined constant in the SI system of units. Improved experimental techniques that, prior to 1983, would have measured the speed of light no longer affect the known value of the speed of light in SI units, but instead allow a more precise realization of the metre by more accurately measuring the wavelength of krypton-86 and other light sources.     The speed of light in a vacuum is exactly c = 299,792,458 m/s. This is not a measured approximation — since 1983, the General Conference on Weights and Measures fixed c at this exact value and redefined the metre accordingly. One metre is now defined as the distance light travels in exactly 1/299,792,458 of a second. [...] What is the speed of light in m/s?

The speed of light in a vacuum is exactly c = 299,792,458 m/s — not an approximation, but a defined value. Since 1983, the metre has been defined so that c is precisely this number. For calculations, c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s (accurate to 0.07%) is sufficient for most physics problems at GCSE, A-Level, or AP Physics level.

 What is the speed of light in km/h? [...] The speed of light is c = 299,792,458 m/s — exactly, not approximately. In round numbers: 3 × 10⁸ m/s, or about 300,000 km/s. In imperial units that is about 186,282 miles per second, or roughly 670.6 million miles per hour (mph). Since 1983 this value has been fixed by definition; the metre is now derived from c, not the other way around. Light covers the Moon's distance in about 1.3 seconds and the Sun's in 8.3 minutes.
